Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "last spring i started planning a june trip to northern michigan for my family, and i noticed how quickly a pleasant idea became a spreadsheet with feelings attached. it would be me, my partner ruth, our daughter june, who is twelve, and our son eli, who is eight. we had six nights available, though two of those nights depended on ruth getting her work schedule confirmed. i wanted the trip to feel unhurried, but i also kept trying to make every day useful, which is not exactly the same thing.

we were looking at a rental near traverse city for the first four nights, then possibly two nights closer to sleeping bear dunes. the second place cost more, and i had not worked out whether moving halfway through the trip would be worth the packing and driving. ruth said, “i don't want us to spend the whole vacation checking in and out.” i agreed with her, but i still saved the listing because it had a small kitchen and a screened porch. the first rental had a kitchen too, but its reviews mentioned road noise, and one reviewer said the upstairs bedrooms got warm.

my first version of the budget put lodging at about $1,450, groceries at $350, and meals out at $300. those were estimates, not amounts we had committed to. i had left gas out because i wanted to check our last few fuel receipts first. i also put $120 in a separate line for parking, beach access, or small fees, even though i did not know which places would charge us. june thought that was too much planning for “a week of looking at water,” while eli wanted to know whether we could rent bikes. i liked that their questions were both about the same trip and almost nothing alike.

1. the plan as it stood in my notes was this, more or less:
   - arrive on saturday, pick up groceries, and keep dinner simple at the rental
   - spend sunday in traverse city, with a farmers market in the morning if we were not too tired
   - choose one beach for monday, but leave the exact beach open until we checked the weather
   - keep tuesday flexible for a short hike or another swim, depending on how the kids felt
   - consider a day trip to sleeping bear dunes on wednesday, provided the drive did not seem like too much
   - use thursday for a second dunes visit or a quieter day near the rental
   - drive home friday, with a stop for lunch somewhere we had not chosen yet

i had written “farmers market” as though we would definitely go, then added “if we're up early” beside it. that small note captured the problem with my plans: i wanted a loose schedule, but i kept filling in the blank spaces. ruth suggested that we pick only one fixed outing each day and let the rest stay open. i thought that sounded sensible. i also worried that, without a plan, we might end up spending the morning asking what everyone wanted to do, then feeling annoyed that the day had disappeared.

there were a few practical questions i could not settle from the listings. one rental said it was a ten-minute walk to the water, but the map showed a road between the house and the shore, and i could not tell whether there was a public path. i saved the host's contact information and drafted a question about it, though i had not sent the message. i wanted to ask whether linens were included, too. the other rental had a clearer description but required a larger deposit, and the cancellation terms looked less flexible. i kept comparing those details as if there were one obvious answer hiding in them.

we talked about food while sorting through the options. june asked if we could make breakfast at the rental instead of eating out every morning, and ruth suggested packing sandwiches for beach days. i wrote down cereal, yogurt, fruit, bread, and peanut butter for the first grocery stop. eli asked for marshmallows, but i had not decided whether we would have access to a fire pit. i was trying to avoid planning every meal, while still wanting to know we would have something easy to eat if we came back tired. that felt like a reasonable middle ground, although the list was already longer than i expected.

one evening i showed everyone the rough itinerary on my laptop. ruth pointed out that the Wednesday drive and a second dunes visit on Thursday might be repetitive, especially if the weather turned. june wanted time to look around the shops in town, and eli returned to the bike question. i said we could look into rentals, but i did not know whether bikes would fit comfortably in the car or whether the kids would still want to ride after a long day outside. i was tempted to settle the question immediately, then realized that there was no need to decide before we knew where we were staying.

what stayed with me was how much of the planning was really about guessing what kind of week we would have. i could compare prices and driving times, but i could not predict our energy, the weather, or whether a beach would feel crowded when we arrived. the trip was still only a set of possibilities in my notes: six nights if the work schedule allowed, a rental we had not chosen, and several activities we might or might not do. i was trying to make room for everyone without turning the week into a checklist, and i had not yet figured out exactly where that balance would land.", "output": "Last spring, I started planning a June trip to northern Michigan for my family, and I noticed how quickly a pleasant idea became a spreadsheet with feelings attached. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "last spring i planned five nights in Quebec City for my family, and this is my review of how the planning went, not a review of one hotel or attraction. it was me, my partner, our kids, who are eight and twelve, and my mother, who joined us for the first three nights. we went in the second week of october, when the leaves were still bright but the evenings got cold fast. i wanted a trip that felt interesting without making every day a march from one reservation to the next. that sounds simple, but with five people and different energy levels it took more work than i expected.

we drove from Albany, and the first planning decision was whether to break up the drive. it is about four and a half hours without stops, according to the route i checked, but we ended up stopping in Burlington for lunch and a walk by the lake. i didn't book a lunch place because my mother has food restrictions and we wanted to choose after seeing what was open. i did reserve a parking space near our rental in Quebec City, which was useful because the streets around it were narrow and busy. the listing said the space was suitable for a midsize car, and our hatchback fit, though opening the rear door fully was awkward.

our rental was in Saint-Roch, not inside the old city walls, and that choice saved money but added some walking. the apartment had two bedrooms, a small kitchen, and a washer-dryer, which mattered because we were packing for five people and didn't want a suitcase for every possible weather change. the stairs were steeper than the photos suggested. my mother managed them slowly, but i would ask about stairs directly before booking again. check-in instructions arrived two days ahead, and the host answered my question about where to leave wet boots within an hour. the message said, “There is a mat by the door, but please keep the hallway clear.” that was clear and helpful, even if we had to shuffle shoes around.

for the days, i made a loose plan in a shared document rather than buying a tour package. my partner likes having a place to start, while the kids do better when they know what comes next. my mother wanted breaks and somewhere to sit that wasn't just a restaurant. i put addresses, opening times, and the nearest bus stop in the document, but i didn't make a minute-by-minute schedule. one museum had shorter hours on monday than the search results first showed, so checking its own page saved us from arriving too late. i had assumed it was open until five, but it closed at four that day.

1. the old city walk was our first full morning. we took the bus uphill and walked back down, which worked better for my mother than doing the climb on foot. we stopped at a bakery near Place Royale for coffee, hot chocolate, and pastries; there were no seats together for all five of us, so we ate outside at a small table and then my mother went inside to warm up. the kids liked the fortifications, but after about an hour they were more interested in finding a place to buy postcards. i was glad we had not booked a guided tour, although a guide might have made the history easier for them to follow.

2. on the second day we visited the Musée de la civilisation and left the afternoon open. the museum had coat storage and enough benches for my mother to rest, and one exhibit kept the kids interested longer than i expected. we had lunch at a counter-service place nearby, where the menu listed ingredients and my mother could ask about her restrictions. after that, my partner and the kids walked along the river while i returned to the apartment with my mother. the weather turned rainy around three, so having a flexible afternoon felt like the right choice. we did not get to the aquarium, which had been on my original list, and nobody was especially disappointed.

3. the last two days were less organized. we had planned a morning at Montmorency Falls, but the forecast kept changing, and we decided not to buy tickets in advance. we went when the rain eased, took the cable car up, and used the covered areas when the wind picked up. the view was impressive, though the paths were slick and we kept the kids close. on our final morning, my mother was already back home, so the four of us went to the market for fruit and maple candy before packing. i had allowed too little time to clean the apartment and load the car, and we left later than planned.

what worked best was making a few firm decisions and leaving room around them. booking the rental and its parking spot early gave me less to worry about, and writing down bus stops meant i wasn't trying to work them out with everyone waiting. the shared document was useful, but the kids rarely looked at it unless i reminded them, so i ended up repeating the day's plan anyway. i would print a small copy next time for my mother, who prefers paper, instead of relying on her phone. i also would pack one extra pair of comfortable shoes for each person. mine got wet on the rainy afternoon, and the apartment dryer took a long time.

overall, the trip felt like a good fit for us, with a few avoidable stresses and no need to see every item on my list. the main weak spot was underestimating transitions: getting five people out the door, finding somewhere to sit, and allowing time to return to the apartment all took longer than the map suggested. i would choose the same neighborhood again because we liked the local bakery and the quieter evenings, but i would check the apartment stairs more carefully and keep the last morning free of errands. my review is positive, though not because everything went exactly to plan; we had enough useful structure to enjoy the city and enough flexibility to change course when the weather or our energy changed.", "output": "Last spring, I planned five nights in Quebec City for my family. Next time, I would print a small copy for my mother, who prefers paper, instead of relying on her phone. I would also pack one extra pair of comfortable shoes for each person.
